Additionally, denote by $F$ the set of points within a distance $r \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B)$ of $A \cup B$. Applying the strong Markov property to $\tau_{F^{\mathsf{c}}}$, we write \begin{multline} \mathbb{P}_x \big( S_{\tau_{A\cup B}} \in B^1 \bigm\vert \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big)\\ \geq \mathbb{E}_x \Big[ \mathbb{P}_{S_{\tau_{F^{\mathsf{c}}}}} \big( S_{\tau_{A \cup B}} \in B^1 \bigm\vert \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big) \mathbb{P}_{S_{\tau_{F^{\mathsf{c}}}}} \big( \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big); \tau_{F^{\mathsf{c}}} < \tau_{A \cup B}\Big]. \end{multline} A standard result (e.g., \cite[Theorem 2.1.3]{lawler2013intersections}) implies that for all sufficiently large $r$, if $y$ belongs to $F^{\mathsf{c}}$, then \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_y \big( S_{\tau_{A \cup B}} \in B^1 \bigm\vert \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big) \geq \frac12 \mathbb{H}_{A \cup B} (B^1). \end{equation} Because $B^1 \cup (A \cup B^2)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lex hm}, \begin{equation} \mathbb{H}_{A \cup B} (B^1) \gtrsim c_1 n^{-\frac{d-1}{d-2}-o_d(1)}. \end{equation} By Lemma~\ref{simple set hit}, for any $y \in F^{\mathsf{c}}$, we have \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_y \big( \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big) \gtrsim \mathrm{dist} (y,A \cup B)^{2-d}. \end{equation} Lastly, by Lemma \ref{lex hm}, the probability of hitting $F^{\mathsf{c}}$ before returning to $A \cup B$ satifies \begin{equation} \mathbb{P}_x (\tau_{F^{\mathsf{c}}} < \tau_{A \cup B} ) \geq \mathrm{esc}_{A\cup B} (x) \gtrsim n^{-\frac{1}{d-2} - o_d(1)}. \end{equation} Applying \eqref{lex cond hit0} through \eqref{lex cond hit3} to \eqref{lex cond hit}, we conclude that \[ \mathbb{P}_x \big( S_{\tau_{A\cup B}} \in B^1 \bigm\vert \tau_{A \cup B} < \infty \big) \gtrsim n^{-\frac{d}{d-2}-o_d(1)} \mathrm{diam} (A \cup B)^{2-d}. \] Here, $o_d(1)$ can be taken to be $1.6$ when $d \geq 5$.

nodes.name: Algorithm A_1: form separated connected clusters
nodes.statement: \small \NoCaptionOfAlgo \DontPrintSemicolon \SetAlgoNoLine \LinesNumbered \SetKwInOut{Input}{Input} \SetKwInOut{Output}{Output} \Input{$U \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}$ and $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$} \Output{$\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}^\times$ that can be lined-up with separation $dn^2 a$} $\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \emptyset, \quad i \leftarrow 1$ \tcp*{Initialize variables.} \While{$U$ is nonempty}{ $\ell \leftarrow \mathrm{lex} (U)$\; $R \leftarrow \mathrm{dist} \big( \ell, U {\setminus} \{\ell \} \big), \quad r \leftarrow 3d(n-i+1)^3 a$\; \tcc{Form a non-isolated lex element if need be.} \While{$R>1$ and $n>1$}{ $x \leftarrow \mu (U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C}), \ell)$ \tcp*{$\ell$ will be replaced by $x$.} \tcc{$x$ either neighbors $U$ \dots} \eIf{$x \in \partial U$}{ $U \leftarrow (U \cup \{x\}) {\setminus} \{\ell\}$ } {\tcc{\dots or one of the existing clusters.} $U \leftarrow U {\setminus} \{\ell\}, \quad j \leftarrow \mathrm{clust} (\mathcal{C},x)$\; $\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{C} \cup^j \{x\}$\; } $\ell \leftarrow \mathrm{lex} (U)$ \tcp*{The lex element of $U$ may have changed.} $R \leftarrow \mathrm{dist} (\ell, U {\setminus} \{\ell\})$\; } \tcc{If the lex element is non-isolated, treadmill it.} \eIf{$R=1$}{ $y \leftarrow \mathrm{expo} (U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C}), \ell)$ \tcp*{$y$ is an exposed neighbor of $\ell$.} $U \leftarrow U {\setminus} \{\ell,y\}$ \tcp*{Remove the pair from $U$.} $\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{C} \cup^i \big\{\ell - r e_1, \ell - (r-1) e_1\big\}$ \tcp*{Treadmill the pair $r$ steps.} $i \leftarrow i + 1$\tcp*{Prepare to form the next cluster.} } {\tcc{Otherwise, $U = \{\ell\}$; add it to an existing cluster.} $x \leftarrow \mu (U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C}), \ell)$ \tcp*{$\ell$ will be replaced by $x$.} $U \leftarrow U {\setminus} \{\ell\},\quad j \leftarrow \mathrm{clust} (\mathcal{C},x)$\; $\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{C} \cup^j \{x\}$\; } } \Return $\mathcal{C}$ \; \caption{Algorithm $\mathcal{A}_1$}

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Consider the tuple of configurations $\mathcal{C}$ in line {\bf 27} of algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg1}}$. As every element of $U$ is eventually treadmilled with another element, or is transported next to another element, every entry of $\mathcal{C}$ is connected and has two or more elements. To prove that $\mathcal{C}$ can be lined-up with separation $r = dn^2 a$, we must additionally show that $\mathcal{C}$ is $2r$ separated. Ignoring those elements that were assigned to clusters in lines {\bf 10} and {\bf 23}, due to line {\bf 19}, clusters $i < j$ are separated by at least \[ 3d(n-i+1)^3 a - 3d(n-j+1)^3 a.\] Because there are at most $[n/2]$ clusters, the preceding expression is at least \[ 3d(n/2+1)^3 a - 3d(n/2)^3 a \geq 2d n^2 a + n.\] At most $n$ elements are added to clusters by executing lines {\bf 10} and {\bf 23}. Because the clusters are connected, the preceding bound implies that the pairwise separation of clusters must be at least $2r = 2dn^2a$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The proof takes the form of an analysis of Algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg1}}$. Denote by $u_{k}$ the configuration $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ after the $k$\textsuperscript{th} time $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ is changed (i.e., an element is moved) by the algorithm. Additionally, denote by $M$ the number of times the configuration changes before the outer {\bf while} loop terminates. To establish \eqref{eq follow alg1}, it suffices to show that there is a sequence of times $t_0 = 0 \leq t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_M \leq N_1$ such that $u_{0} = U$, $u_{M} = \pi \big( \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg1}} (U,a) \big)$, and \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_0} \big( U_{t_1} = u_1, U_{t_2} = u_2, \dots, U_{t_M} = u_{M} \big) \geq p_1. \end{equation} We will argue that $M \leq n(n+1)$, that we can take $t_M = n(n+1)r_1$ for $r_1 = 3dn^3 a$, and that \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} \big( U_{t_k} = u_k \big) \geq q, \end{equation} for each $k \in \{1,\dots,M\}$, for a constant $q = q(a,d,n) > 0$. The Markov property then implies that \eqref{alg bd1} holds with $N_1 = n(n+1)r_1$ and $p_1 = q^{n(n+1)}$. {\em Claim 1}. We claim that $M \leq n(n+1)$. Observe that the outer and inner {\bf while} loops starting on lines {\bf 2} and {\bf 5} each repeat at most $n$ times. Indeed, $U$ loses an element every time the outer loop repeats, which can happen no more than $n$ times. Concerning the inner loop, no non-isolated element is made to be isolated, while, each time line {\bf 6} is executed, the isolated element $\ell$ is replaced by an element $x$ which is non-isolated. This can happen at most $n$ times consecutively. Accordingly, $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes at most $n+1$ times every time the outer loop repeats, hence $M \leq n (n+1)$. {\em Claim 2}. We now claim that we can take $t_M = n(n+1)r_1$. It suffices to argue that, each time $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes, at most $r_1$ steps of HAT are required to realize the change. The configuration $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes due to the execution of lines {\bf 8}, {\bf 10} and {\bf 11}, {\bf 18} and {\bf 19}, or {\bf 23} and {\bf 24}. In all but one case---that of lines {\bf 18} and {\bf 19}---the transition requires only one HAT step. For lines {\bf 18} and {\bf 19}, at most $r_1$ steps are needed. Because there are at most $n(n+1)$ changes, $t_M$ can be taken to be $n(n+1)r_1$. {\em Claim 3}. We now verify \eqref{alg bd22} by considering each way $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ can change and by bounding below the probability that it is realized by HAT. Assume $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ has changed $k-1$ times so far. \begin{itemize} \item Lines {\bf 8}, {\bf 10} and {\bf 11}, or {\bf 23} and {\bf 24}: Activation at $\ell$ and transport to $x$. Assume that $a$ is sufficiently large in $d$ and $n$ to exceed the constant $r$ in the statement of Lemma \ref{lex hm}. Then, since $\ell$ is the lex element of $U$ and since $\mathrm{dist} (U, \pi (\mathcal{C})) \geq a$, we can apply Lemma \ref{lex hm} with $A = U$ and $B = \pi (\mathcal{C})$ to find that \begin{equation} \mathbb{H}_{U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})}(\ell) \geq h, \end{equation} for a positive number $h = h(d,n)$. By the definition of $\mu$, $x$ is the most likely destination of an element activated at $\ell$. Transport from $\ell$ occurs to at most $2dn$ sites and so, by the pigeonhole principle, the element from $\ell$ is transported to $x$ with a probability of at least $(2dn)^{-1}$. Together, these bounds imply that \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} \big( U_{t_k} = u_k \big) \geq h (2dn)^{-1}. \end{equation} \item Lines {\bf 18} and {\bf 19}: Treadmilling of $\{\ell,y\}$. In the first step, we activate at $y$ and transport to $\ell-e_1$. While $y$ is not lex in $U$, by the definition of $\mathrm{expo}$, it is an exposed neighbor of $\ell$. Because $\mathrm{dist} (U, \pi (\mathcal{C})) \geq a$, if $a$ is at least $4^d n$, we can apply Lemma \ref{lem hm comp} with $A = U$ and $B = \pi (\mathcal{C})$ to conclude that $\mathbb{H}_{U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})} (y)$ is at least $c_1 h$ from \eqref{h lw bd}, for a positive number $c_1 = c_1 (d,n)$. Additionally, Lemma \ref{kesten cor} implies that an element activated at $y$ is transported to $\ell-e_1$ with a probability of at least $c_2 = c_2 (d,n)$. Consequently, denoting \[ v_1 = \big( u_{k-1} \cup \{\ell-e_1,\ell\} \big) {\setminus} \{\ell,y\}, \] we have \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} (U_1 = v_1) \geq c_1 c_2 h. \end{equation} Now, consider the configuration $v_m$ resulting from starting at $u_{k-1}$ and treadmilling $\{\ell,y\}$ a total of $m \geq 2$ steps in the $-e_1$ direction: \[ v_m = \big( u_{k-1} \cup \{\ell-me_1, \ell - (m-1)e_1\} \big) {\setminus} \{\ell,y\}.\] To obtain $v_{m+1}$, we activate at $\ell-(m-1)e_1$ and transport to $\ell-(m+1)e_1$. By the same reasoning as before, \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{v_m} \big( U_1 = v_{m+1} \big) \geq c_1c_2 h. \end{equation} By \eqref{claim3 bd2}, \eqref{claim3 bd3}, and the Markov property, \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} \big( U_{t_k} = u_k \big) \geq \big(c_1 c_2 h \big)^{r_1}. \end{equation} \end{itemize} The bounds \eqref{claim3 bd1} and \eqref{claim3 bd4} show that, whenever $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes, the change can be realized by HAT (in one or more steps) with a probability of at least \[ q = \min \big\{ h (2dn)^{-1}, (c_1c_2h)^{r_1} \big\}. \] This proves \eqref{alg bd22}. We complete the proof by combining claims 1--3. Note that, to apply Lemma~\ref{lem hm comp} and Lemma~\ref{lex hm}, we assumed that $a$ was at least $\alpha_1 \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, where $\alpha_1$ is an integer which is at least $4^d n$ and the constant $r = r(d,n)$ from Lemma~\ref{lex hm}.

This can happen at most $n$ times consecutively. Accordingly, $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes at most $n+1$ times every time the outer loop repeats, hence $M \leq n (n+1)$.

nodes.name: Claim 3: each change has probability at least q
nodes.statement:
{\em Claim 3}. We now verify \eqref{alg bd22} by considering each way $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ can change and by bounding below the probability that it is realized by HAT. Assume $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ has changed $k-1$ times so far.
\begin{itemize}
\item Lines {\bf 8}, {\bf 10} and {\bf 11}, or {\bf 23} and {\bf 24}: Activation at $\ell$ and transport to $x$. Assume that $a$ is sufficiently large in $d$ and $n$ to exceed the constant $r$ in the statement of Lemma \ref{lex hm}. Then, since $\ell$ is the lex element of $U$ and since $\mathrm{dist} (U, \pi (\mathcal{C})) \geq a$, we can apply Lemma \ref{lex hm} with $A = U$ and $B = \pi (\mathcal{C})$ to find that
\begin{equation} \mathbb{H}_{U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})}(\ell) \geq h,
\end{equation}
for a positive number $h = h(d,n)$. By the definition of $\mu$, $x$ is the most likely destination of an element activated at $\ell$. Transport from $\ell$ occurs to at most $2dn$ sites and so, by the pigeonhole principle, the element from $\ell$ is transported to $x$ with a probability of at least $(2dn)^{-1}$. Together, these bounds imply that
\begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} \big( U_{t_k} = u_k \big) \geq h (2dn)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
\item Lines {\bf 18} and {\bf 19}: Treadmilling of $\{\ell,y\}$. In the first step, we activate at $y$ and transport to $\ell-e_1$. While $y$ is not lex in $U$, by the definition of $\mathrm{expo}$, it is an exposed neighbor of $\ell$. Because $\mathrm{dist} (U, \pi (\mathcal{C})) \geq a$, if $a$ is at least $4^d n$, we can apply Lemma \ref{lem hm comp} with $A = U$ and $B = \pi (\mathcal{C})$ to conclude that $\mathbb{H}_{U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})} (y)$ is at least $c_1 h$ from \eqref{h lw bd}, for a positive number $c_1 = c_1 (d,n)$. Additionally, Lemma \ref{kesten cor} implies that an element activated at $y$ is transported to $\ell-e_1$ with a probability of at least $c_2 = c_2 (d,n)$. Consequently, denoting
\[
v_1 = \big( u_{k-1} \cup \{\ell-e_1,\ell\} \big) {\setminus} \{\ell,y\},
\]
we have
\begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} (U_1 = v_1) \geq c_1 c_2 h.
\end{equation}

Now, consider the configuration $v_m$ resulting from starting at $u_{k-1}$ and treadmilling $\{\ell,y\}$ a total of $m \geq 2$ steps in the $-e_1$ direction:
\[ v_m = \big( u_{k-1} \cup \{\ell-me_1, \ell - (m-1)e_1\} \big) {\setminus} \{\ell,y\}.\]
To obtain $v_{m+1}$, we activate at $\ell-(m-1)e_1$ and transport to $\ell-(m+1)e_1$. By the same reasoning as before,
\begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{v_m} \big( U_1 = v_{m+1} \big) \geq c_1c_2 h.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{claim3 bd2}, \eqref{claim3 bd3}, and the Markov property,
\begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} \big( U_{t_k} = u_k \big) \geq \big(c_1 c_2 h \big)^{r_1}.
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}

The bounds \eqref{claim3 bd1} and \eqref{claim3 bd4} show that, whenever $U \cup \pi (\mathcal{C})$ changes, the change can be realized by HAT (in one or more steps) with a probability of at least
\[ q = \min \big\{ h (2dn)^{-1}, (c_1c_2h)^{r_1} \big\}. \]
This proves \eqref{alg bd22}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim 3: each change has probability at least q

nodes.statement: \small \NoCaptionOfAlgo \DontPrintSemicolon \SetAlgoNoLine \LinesNumbered \SetKwInOut{Input}{Input} \SetKwInOut{Output}{Output} \Input{$\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}^\times$ that can be lined-up with separation $dn^2 a$, for some $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$.} \Output{$\mathcal{L}(C)$ \eqref{lined up tuple}.} \For{$i \in \{1,\dots,\# \mathcal{C}\}$}{ $\ell_i \leftarrow \mathrm{lex} (\mathcal{C}^i)$ \tcp*{The segment will grow from $\ell_i$.} \For{$j \in \{1,\dots,|\mathcal{C}^i|-1\}$}{ $x_j \leftarrow \mathrm{lex} \big( \big\{ z \in \mathcal{C}^i {\setminus} \{\ell_i + L_j\}: \mathbb{H}_{\pi (\mathcal{C})} (z) > 0 \big\} \big)$ \tcp*{$x_j$ is lex among exposed elements of $\mathcal{C}^i$ which have not yet been added to the growing segment.} $y_j \leftarrow \ell_i - j e_1$ \tcp*{$y_j$ is the next addition to the segment.} $\mathcal{C} \leftarrow (\mathcal{C} \sd{i} \{x_j\}) \cup^i \{y_j\}$ \tcp*{Update the $i$\textsuperscript{th} cluster.} } } \Return $\mathcal{C}$ \caption{Algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg2}}$}

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The only way that the algorithm could fail to produce $\mathcal{L} (\mathcal{C})$ is if, for some outer {\bf for} loop $i$ and inner {\bf for} loop $j$, the assignment in line {\bf 5} is impossible. This would mean that no element of $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{C}^i {\setminus} \{\ell_i + L_j\}$ was exposed in $\pi (\mathcal{C})$. While there must be an element of $\mathcal{D}$ which is exposed in $\mathcal{C}^i$, the elements of $\mathcal{C}^{\neq i}$ could, in principle, separate $\mathcal{D}$ from $\infty$. In fact, as we argue now, this cannot occur because the clusters remain far enough apart while the algorithm runs. Each $\mathcal{C}^i$ remains connected while the algorithm runs, so there is a ball $B_i$ of radius $n$ which contains $\mathcal{C}^i$. The $B_i$ are finite and $\ast$-connected, so each $\ast$-visible boundary $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$ is connected by Lemma~\ref{kesten result}. Moreover, each $\partial_{\mathrm{vis}} B_i$ is disjoint from $\cup_j B_j$ because $\mathrm{dist} (B_i, B_j)$ exceeds $\sqrt{d}$. This lower bound holds because the clusters are initially $2dn^2 a$ separated and the separation decreases by at most one with each of the $n$ loops of the algorithm, hence \[ \mathrm{dist} (B^i, B^j) \geq \mathrm{dist} (\mathcal{C}^i, \mathcal{C}^j) - \mathrm{diam} (B_i) - \mathrm{diam} (B_j) - n \geq 2dn^2 a - 5n > \sqrt{d}. \] The rest of the argument, which constructs an infinite path from $\mathcal{D}$ which otherwise avoids $\mathcal{C}$, is identical to the corresponding step in the proof of Proposition~\ref{help for at pairs}. We conclude that some element of $\mathcal{D}$ is exposed in $\pi (\mathcal{C})$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Clusters stay far apart, so the visible-boundary rerouting argument of Proposition 7.4 gives an exposed element.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Given a tuple $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}^\times$ that satisfies the hypotheses, algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg2}}$ specifies for each cluster $i$ a sequence of $|\mathcal{C}^i|-1$ pairs $(x_j,y_j)$, where $x_j$ is the site of activation and $y_j$ is the site to which transport occurs, to rearrange $\mathcal{C}^i$ into $\mathrm{lex} (\mathcal{C}^i) + L_{|\mathcal{C}^i|}$. We note that no pair will result in a decrease in cluster separation of more than one, or an increase in cluster diameter of more than one. Because the clusters are initially $2 dn^2 a$ separated, the clusters will remain $2dn^2 a - n \geq a$ separated throughout. Let $\alpha_2$ be an integer at least as large as $4^dn$ and the constant $r$ from Lemma~\ref{lex hm}. Accordingly, if $a \geq \mathbb{Z}_{\geq \alpha_2}$, then the combination of Lemma \ref{lem hm comp} and Lemma \ref{lex hm} implies that there is a constant $h = h (d,n)$ such that each $x_j$ can be activated with a probability of at least $h$. Moreover, Lemma~\ref{kesten cor} implies that there is a positive number $c = c (d,n)$ such that an element from $x_j$ can be transported to $y_j$ with a probability of at least $c$. Consequently, denoting $\mathcal{C}' = (\mathcal{C} \sd{i} \{x_j\}) \cup^i \{y_j\}$, the transition in line {\bf 7} occurs with a probability of at least \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{\pi (\mathcal{C})} \big( U_1 = \pi (\mathcal{C}') \big) \geq c h. \end{equation} By \eqref{a2 bd1} and the Markov property, and the fact that there are at most $n$ pairs, we have \[ \mathbf{P}_{\pi (\mathcal{C})} \Big( U_n = \pi \big( \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg2}} (\mathcal{C}) \big) \Big) \geq (ch)^n. \] Taking $p_2 = (ch)^n$ gives \eqref{eq rearrange small}.

nodes.statement: \small \NoCaptionOfAlgo \DontPrintSemicolon \SetAlgoNoLine \LinesNumbered \SetKwInOut{Input}{Input} \SetKwInOut{Output}{Output} \Input{$\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C})$ \eqref{lined up tuple}, for $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}^\times$ that can be lined-up with separation $n^2 a$, for some $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$.} \Output{An $(a,2 (\log a)^{-1})$ DOT clustering $\mathcal{D}$ in $\mathrm{Ref}^\times$.} $k \leftarrow 1$ \tcp*{$k$ counts the number of new clusters.} \For{$i \in \{1,\dots,\# \mathcal{D}\}$}{ \For{$j \in \{1,\dots,[|\mathcal{D}^i|/2]-1\}$}{ $\ell \leftarrow \mathrm{lex} (\mathcal{D}^i),\quad r \leftarrow 2(n-j)a$\; $\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \big( \mathcal{D} \sd{i} \{\ell,\ell+e_1\} \big) \cup^{\# \mathcal{D} +k} \{\ell - re_1, \ell - (r-1)e_1\}$ \tcp*{Treadmill the pair $r$ steps, labeling it as cluster $\# \mathcal{D}+k$.} $k \leftarrow k+1$ \tcp*{Account for the creation of a new cluster.} } } \Return $\mathcal{D}$ \caption{Algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}}$}

nodes.name: Three properties to verify
nodes.statement: To prove that $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}} (\mathcal{D}_0,a)$ is an $(a,2(\log a)^{-1})$ DOT clustering in $\mathrm{Ref}^\times$, we will verify that $\mathcal{D}_M$ satisfies the DOT condition \eqref{two or three elems}, that $\mathrm{sep} (\mathcal{D}_M) \geq a$, and that each cluster of $\mathcal{D}_M$ is a connected line segment parallel to $e_1$. These conditions imply that the $(a,b)$ separation conditions \eqref{abs rel sep} hold with this $a$ and $b = 2(\log a)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Three properties to verify

nodes.name: Clusters are connected segments of two or three elements
nodes.statement: Concerning \eqref{two or three elems} and the claim that each cluster of $\mathcal{D}_M^i$ is a connected line segment parallel to $e_1$, we note that line {\bf 5} creates connected clusters of size two and, because it is executed $[ |\mathcal{D}^i|/2 ] - 1$ times for cluster $i$, when the inner {\bf for} loop ends on line {\bf 7}, only two or three (connected) elements of the original cluster $\mathcal{D}^i$ remain. Accordingly, every cluster of $\mathcal{D}_M$ has two or three elements and is connected. It is clear from line {\bf 5} that, since the clusters of $\mathcal{D}_0$ are line segments parallel to $e_1$, this is also true of $\mathcal{D}_M$.
nodes.statement_short: Clusters are connected segments of two or three elements

We conclude that $\mathcal{D}_M$ is an $(a,b)$ DOT clustering in $\mathrm{Ref}^\times$.
nodes.statement_short: Diameter condition with b = 2/log a

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Proposition \ref{alg3 works}, denote by $\mathcal{D}_k$ the clustering $\mathcal{D}_0 = \mathcal{L} (\mathcal{C})$ once it has been changed by the algorithm for the $k$\textsuperscript{th} time (i.e., the $k$\textsuperscript{th} time line {\bf 5} is executed). Denote by $M$ the number of times algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}}$ changes $\mathcal{D}_0$. Call $u_k = \pi (\mathcal{D}_k)$. To establish \eqref{eq rearrange small2}, it suffices to show that there is a sequence of times $t_0 = 0 \leq t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_M \leq N_3$ such that $u_{0} = U$, $u_{M} = \pi \big( \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}} (\mathcal{D}_0,a) \big)$, and \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_0} \big( U_{t_1} = u_1, U_{t_2} = u_2, \dots, U_{t_M} = u_{M} \big) \geq p_3. \end{equation} Consider outer {\bf for} loop $i$, inner {\bf for} loop $j$, and suppose that $\mathcal{D}_0$ has been changed a total of $k-1$ times thus far. Let $r = 2(n-j)a$. We will first bound below the probability that HAT realizes $u_k$ as $U_{r}$ from $u_{k-1}$ (i.e., the transition reflected in line {\bf 5}). HAT can realize this transition by treadmilling the elements at $\ell = \mathrm{lex} (\mathcal{D}_{k-1}^i)$ and $\ell+e_1$ to $\{\ell - re_1,\ell-(r-1)e_1\}$. For example, in the first step, we activate at $\ell+e_1$ and transport to $\ell-e_1$. As observed in the proof of Proposition \ref{alg3 works}, $\mathcal{D}_k$ is $a$ separated for every $0 \leq k \leq M$. Denote by $\alpha_3$ an integer at least as large as $4^d n$ and the constant $r$ from Lemma~\ref{lex hm}. If $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq \alpha_3}$, then the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lem hm comp} and Lemma \ref{lex hm} are satisfied with $A = \pi (\mathcal{D}_k^i)$ and $B = \pi (\mathcal{D}_k^{\neq i})$, and they together imply the existence of a positive lower bound $h = h(d,n)$ on $\mathbb{H}_{u_{k-1}} (\ell+e_1)$. It is clear that the element at $\ell+e_1$ can be transported to $\ell-e_1$ with a probability of at least $c = c(d)$, and so, denoting \[ v_s = \big( u_{k-1} \cup \{\ell-s e_1,\ell - (s-1) e_1 \} \big) {\setminus} \{ \ell,\ell+e_1\}, \] we have \begin{equation*} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} ( U_1 = v_1 ) \geq ch. \end{equation*} We can simply repeat this argument with $\ell$ and $\ell-e_1$ in the place of $\ell+e_1$ and $\ell$, then $\ell-e_1$ and $\ell-2e_1$, and so on. With the choice $u_k = v_r$, the Markov property implies \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_{k-1}} (U_{r} = u_k) \geq (ch)^{r}. \end{equation} The same bound \eqref{alg3 bd3} holds for any $k \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, so, by another use of the Markov property and the fact that $M \leq n$, we find \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{u_0} \big( U_{r} = u_1, U_{2r} = u_2, \dots, U_{Mr} = u_M \big) \geq (ch)^{rn}. \end{equation} This proves \eqref{alg3 bd1} with $N_3 = nr$ and $p_3 = (ch)^{rn}$.
nodes.statement_short: Realize each treadmill of r steps with probability (ch)^r and chain with the Markov property.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $U \in \mathrm{Conf}_{d,n}$. It suffices to prove the result when $a$ is sufficiently large, because if $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a,1}^\bullet$ and $0 < a' \leq a$, then $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a',1}^\bullet$. With this in mind, denote by $\alpha = \alpha (d,n)$ the largest of the integers $\alpha_1$ through $\alpha_3$ in Propositions \ref{follow alg1}, \ref{rearrange small}, and \ref{break lines}, and assume that $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq \alpha}$. By Proposition \ref{follow alg1}, there are positive numbers $N_1 = N_1 (a,d,n)$ and $p_1 = p_1 (a,d,n)$ such that \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_U \Big( U_{N_1} = \pi \big(\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg1}} (U, a) \big) \Big) \geq p_1. \end{equation} By Proposition \ref{alg1 works}, $\mathcal{C}_1 = \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg1}} (U, a)$ can be lined-up with separation $d n^2 a$. Consequently, by Proposition \ref{rearrange small}, there is a positive number $p_2 = p_2 (d,n)$ such that \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{\pi (\mathcal{C}_1)} \Big( U_{n} = \pi \big( \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg2}} (\mathcal{C}_1) \big) \Big) \geq p_2. \end{equation} By Proposition \ref{alg2 works}, $\mathcal{C}_2$ equals $\mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg2}} (\mathcal{C}_1) = \mathcal{L} (\mathcal{C}_1)$. Since $\mathcal{C}_2$ is $n^2 a$ separated, by Proposition \ref{break lines}, there are positive numbers $N_3 = N_3 (a,d,n)$ and $p_3 = p_3 (a,d,n)$ such that \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_{\pi (\mathcal{C}_2)} \Big( U_{N_3} = \pi \big( \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}} (\mathcal{C}_2,a) \big) \Big) \geq p_3. \end{equation} Denote $\mathcal{C}_3 = \mathcal{A}_{\ref{alg3}} (\mathcal{C}_2,a)$. By the Markov property and \eqref{thm14 conc1} through \eqref{thm14 conc3}, \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}_U \big( U_{N_1+n+N_3} = \pi (\mathcal{C}_3) \big) \geq p_1 p_2 p_3. \end{equation} By Proposition \ref{alg3 works}, $\mathcal{C}_3 \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a,b}^\bullet \cap \mathrm{Ref}^\times$ with $b = 2 (\log a)^{-1}$. Note that $a \geq 4^d n$ (the constant in Lemma~\ref{lem hm comp}), so $b < 1$. Because $\mathcal{C}_3$ is $(a,b)$ separated for $b < 1$, it is also $(a,1)$ separated. Setting $N = N_1+n+N_3$ and $p = p_1 p_2 p_3$ concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $a$ be the smallest integer that is larger than the constants denoted $r = r(d,n)$ in Lemma \ref{lex hm} and Lemma \ref{lex hm2}. By Theorem \ref{thm form dot}, there is a positive integer $M = M(d,n)$ and a positive number $q = q (d,n)$, such that there exists $\mathcal{C} \in \mathrm{Clust}_{a+n,1}^\bullet (U_M)$. Let $\ell$ be the lex element of $U_M$, which we assume w.l.o.g.\@ belongs to $\mathcal{C}^1$. Because $\mathcal{C}$ is $a+n$ separated, we can activate any lex element of any cluster with a probability of at least $q_2 = q_2 (d,n) > 0$ by Lemma \ref{lex hm}. Then, by Lemma \ref{lex hm2}, we can transport to $\ell-e_1$ with a probability of at least $q_3 = q_3 (d,n, \mathrm{diam} (V))$. Reassigning the element at $\ell-e_1$ to cluster $\mathcal{C}^1$, the resulting clusters are at least $a + n-1$ separated. Because the resulting clusters are still $a$ separated, we can simply repeat this process, transporting an element to $\ell-2e_1$, and so on. Continuing in this fashion for a total of $n$ steps results in $U_{M+n} = \ell + L_n$. The preceding discussion and the Markov property imply \[ \mathbf{P}_V \big( \widehat U_{M+n} = \widehat L_n \big) \geq q_1 (q_2 q_3)^n.\] Setting $N_4 = M+n$ and $p_4 = q_1 (q_2 q_3)^n$ gives \eqref{eq cor line}.

Because $\mathcal{C}$ is $a+n$ separated, we can activate any lex element of any cluster with a probability of at least $q_2 = q_2 (d,n) > 0$ by Lemma \ref{lex hm}. Then, by Lemma \ref{lex hm2}, we can transport to $\ell-e_1$ with a probability of at least $q_3 = q_3 (d,n, \mathrm{diam} (V))$. Reassigning the element at $\ell-e_1$ to cluster $\mathcal{C}^1$, the resulting clusters are at least $a + n-1$ separated.

Because the resulting clusters are still $a$ separated, we can simply repeat this process, transporting an element to $\ell-2e_1$, and so on. Continuing in this fashion for a total of $n$ steps results in $U_{M+n} = \ell + L_n$. The preceding discussion and the Markov property imply
\[ \mathbf{P}_V \big( \widehat U_{M+n} = \widehat L_n \big) \geq q_1 (q_2 q_3)^n.\]
Setting $N_4 = M+n$ and $p_4 = q_1 (q_2 q_3)^n$ gives \eqref{eq cor line}.

nodes.name: Inductive construction of a configuration from a line segment
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 2$ and let $V \in \mathrm{NonIso}_{d,n}$. In terms of $r = [\, \mathrm{rad} (V)\,]$, there are positive integers $M = 4^d n^2 r$ and $\ell = M/n$, and a sequence $( (x_i,y_i) )_{i=1}^M$ in $\mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{Z}^d$ such that, setting \[ W_0 = L_n \quad \text{and} \quad W_j = (W_{j-1} {\setminus} \{x_j\}) \cup \{y_j\}, \quad 1 \leq j \leq M, \] the following conclusions hold: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $W_M = V$. \item[(ii)] For each $1 \leq j \leq M$, $x_j$ is exposed in $W_{j-1}$. \item[(iii)] For each $1 \leq j \leq M$, there is a path $\Gamma_j$ from $x_j$ to $y_j$, which lies outside of $W_{j-1} {\setminus} \{x_j\}$ but inside of $B (r+dn)$, and which has a length of at most $\ell$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Any non-isolated configuration is reachable from the segment $L_n$ by M explicit moves with exposed activations and short transport paths in a bounded ball.
conclusions: For each $1 \leq j \leq M$, $x_j$ is exposed in $W_{j-1}$
For each $1 \leq j \leq M$, there is a path $\Gamma_j$ from $x_j$ to $y_j$, which lies outside of $W_{j-1} {\setminus} \{x_j\}$ but inside of $B (r+dn)$, and which has a length of at most $\ell$
nodes.label: induc arg

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By conclusion (iii) of Proposition~\ref{induc arg}, for each $1 \leq j \leq M$, we have $W_{j-1} \subseteq B(r + d n)$. By this observation and conclusion (ii), the activation component $\mathbb{H}_{W_{j-1}} (x_j)$ of each transition is at least a positive number $q_1 = q_1 (d,n,r)$. Again, by (iii), there is a path $\Gamma_j$, with a length of at most $\ell$, which can realize the transport step from $x_j$ to $y_j$. Consequently, in terms of $\tau = \tau_{W_{j-1} {\setminus} \{x_j\}}$, the transport component $\mathbb{P}_{x_j} ( S_{\tau - 1} = y_j \mid \tau < \infty)$ of each transition is at least $q_2 = (2d)^{-\ell-1}$. By the Markov property and conclusion (i), the probability in \eqref{line to set} is at least the product of these components, over $M$ steps: \[ \mathbf{P}_{L_n} \big( \widehat{U}_M = \widehat{V} \big) \geq (q_1 q_2)^M. \]
nodes.statement_short: Each prescribed move has activation bounded below in a bounded ball and transport along a short path; multiply over M steps.

nodes.name: Activation components bounded below
nodes.statement: By conclusion (iii) of Proposition~\ref{induc arg}, for each $1 \leq j \leq M$, we have $W_{j-1} \subseteq B(r + d n)$. By this observation and conclusion (ii), the activation component $\mathbb{H}_{W_{j-1}} (x_j)$ of each transition is at least a positive number $q_1 = q_1 (d,n,r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Activation components bounded below

nodes.name: Transport components bounded below
nodes.statement: Again, by (iii), there is a path $\Gamma_j$, with a length of at most $\ell$, which can realize the transport step from $x_j$ to $y_j$. Consequently, in terms of $\tau = \tau_{W_{j-1} {\setminus} \{x_j\}}$, the transport component $\mathbb{P}_{x_j} ( S_{\tau - 1} = y_j \mid \tau < \infty)$ of each transition is at least $q_2 = (2d)^{-\ell-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport components bounded below

nodes.name: Multiply over M steps
nodes.statement:
By the Markov property and conclusion (i), the probability in \eqref{line to set} is at least the product of these components, over $M$ steps:
\[
\mathbf{P}_{L_n} \big( \widehat{U}_M = \widehat{V} \big) \geq (q_1 q_2)^M.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply over M steps

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The base case of $n=2$ is trivial because $\mathrm{\widehat{N}onIso}_{d,2}$ has the same elements as the equivalence class $\widehat{L}_2$. Now suppose the claim holds up to $n-1$ for $n \geq 3$. There are two cases, which we phrase in terms of the ``exposed'' boundary of $V$: \[ \partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V = \{x \in V: \mathbb{H}_V (x) > 0\}.\] \begin{enumerate} \item There is a non-isolated $x \in \partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$ such that $V{\setminus}\{x\} \in \mathrm{NonIso}_{d,n-1}$. \item For every non-isolated $x \in \partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$, $V {\setminus} \{x\} \in \mathrm{Iso}_{d,n-1}$. \end{enumerate} {\em Case 1}. Peform the following steps. In what follows, denote $r = [\mathrm{rad} (V)]+1$. \begin{itemize} \item[Step 1:] {\em ``Treadmill'' a pair of elements in the $-e_1$ direction for $m = r + dn - 2$ steps.} Specifically, activate the element $e_1$ and transport it to $-e_1$, then activate the element at the origin and transport it to $-2e_1$, followed by activation at $-e_1$ and transport to $-3e_1$, and so on. \item[Step 2:] {\em Isolate an element outside of $B(r+ dn-2)$.} At the end of Step 1, an element lies at $-m e_1$ and another at $-(m-1)e_1$. Activate the latter and transport it to the $e_1$, then activate the element at $(n-1)e_1$ and transport it to the origin. \item[Step 3:] {\em Use the induction hypothesis to form $(V{\setminus}\{x\}) \cup \{-m e_1\}$, for a particular $x$.} By the end of Step 2, the configuration is $L_{n-1} \cup \{-m e_1\}$. We use the induction hypothesis to form $V {\setminus} \{x\}$ from the $L_{n-1}$ subset, where $x$ is a non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$ such that $V {\setminus} \{x\} \in \mathrm{NonIso}_{d,n-1}$. The use of the induction hypothesis guarantees that there is a sequence of $4^d(n-1)^2 r$ HAT steps from $L_{n-1}$, which: (i) result in $(V{\setminus}\{x\}) \cup \{-m e_1\}$; (ii) have positive activation components; and (iii) have transport steps that are realized by random walk paths with lengths of at most $4^d (n-1) r$, which remain inside $B(r+d(n-1))$. \item[Step 4:] {\em Transport the element at $-m e_1$ to $x$.} We activate the element at $-m e_1$ and transport it to $x$, which is possible because $x$ is non-isolated and exposed in $V$. Because $V{\setminus}\{x\}$ lies in $B(r)$, Lemma \ref{kesten cor} implies that there is a path from $-m e_1$ to $x$ which avoids $V{\setminus}\{x\}$, has a length of at most $\ell = 4^d n r$, and lies in $B(r+dn-1)$. \end{itemize} Note that Steps 1 and 2 require $r+dn$ HAT steps, the activation components of which are positive and the transport components of which can be realized by paths of length at most $r+dn \leq \ell$. Steps 3 and 4 require $4^d(n-1)^2 r + 1$ HAT steps, again with positive activation components and transport components realized by paths of length at most $\ell$. In total, at most $M = 4^d n^2 r$ HAT steps are needed and, since all paths lie in $B(r+dn-1)$, conclusions (i) through (iii) hold. {\em Case 2}. Because we cannot remove a non-isolated element of $V$ without obtaining an isolated set---a set to which the induction hypothesis does not apply---we must instead use the induction hypothesis to form a set related to $V$. In fact, the first two steps are the same as in Case 1, so we begin with the configuration $L_{n-1} \cup \{-m e_1\}$ and specify the third and subsequent steps. \begin{itemize} \item[Step 3':] {\em Use the induction hypothesis.} Let $w$ and $y$ be the least and greatest elements of $V$ in the lexicographic order, and let $x$ be any non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$. We use the induction hypothesis to form \[ V' = (V {\setminus} \{x,y\}) \cup \{w-e_1\}, \] which is possible because $V' \in \mathrm{\widehat{N}onIso}_{d,n-1}$. The result is a sequence of $4^d(n-1)^2 r$ HAT steps from $L_{n-1}$ which form $V' \cup \{-m e_1\}$ with positive activation components and transport components which are realized by random walk paths with the same properties as in Step 3. \item[Step 4':] {\em Activate the element at $-m e_1$ and transport it to $w-2e_1$.} \item[Step 5':] {\em Treadmill the pair $\{w-e_1,w-2e_1\}$.} Since $w$ is the least element of $V$ in the lexicographic order, $w-e_1$ and $w-2e_1$ are the only elements which lie in $O_1 = \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: z \cdot e_1 \leq w \cdot e_1\}$. Similarly, due to the choice of $y$, it is the only element which lies in $O_2 = \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: z \cdot e_d \geq y \cdot e_d\}$. Consequently, it is possible to treadmill the pair $\{w-e_1,w-2e_1\}$ to: \begin{itemize} \item $B(r+3)^{\mathsf{c}}$ without leaving $O_1$; then \item $O_2$ without leaving $B(r+6) {\setminus} B(r + 3)$; and \item $\{y,y+e_d\}$ without leaving $O_2$. \end{itemize} This requires at most $f_2 = 10 r$ HAT steps, each of which has a positive activation component and a transport component realized by a random walk path of length five. \item[Step 6':] {\em Activate at $\{y+e_d\}$ and transport to $x$.} The configuration at the end of Step 5' is $(V {\setminus} \{x\}) \cup \{y+e_d\}$, so activating the element at $\{y+e_d\}$ and transporting it to $x$ (which is possible because $x$ is an exposed, non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$), forms $V$. \end{itemize} Recall that Steps 1 and 2 require $r+dn$ HAT steps, which can be realized by paths of length at most $r+dn \leq \ell$. Steps 3' and 4' require $4^d(n-1)^2r + 1$ HAT steps, realized by paths of length at most $\ell$. Steps 5' and 6' require $10r+1$ HAT steps, with paths satisfying the same length bound. All activation components are positive. At most $M$ HAT steps are needed in total and, since all paths lie in $B(r+dn-1)$, conclusions (i) through (iii) hold.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n with two cases depending on whether removing an exposed element keeps the set non-isolated. Elements are treadmilled out, the rest is formed by induction, and the spare element is moved into place.

nodes.name: Case 1 construction
nodes.statement:
{\em Case 1}. Peform the following steps. In what follows, denote $r = [\mathrm{rad} (V)]+1$.
 \begin{itemize}
 \item[Step 1:] {\em ``Treadmill'' a pair of elements in the $-e_1$ direction for $m = r + dn - 2$ steps.} Specifically, activate the element $e_1$ and transport it to $-e_1$, then activate the element at the origin and transport it to $-2e_1$, followed by activation at $-e_1$ and transport to $-3e_1$, and so on.  

 \item[Step 2:] {\em Isolate an element outside of $B(r+ dn-2)$.} At the end of Step 1, an element lies at $-m e_1$ and another at $-(m-1)e_1$. Activate the latter and transport it to the $e_1$, then activate the element at $(n-1)e_1$ and transport it to the origin. 

 \item[Step 3:] {\em Use the induction hypothesis to form $(V{\setminus}\{x\}) \cup \{-m e_1\}$, for a particular $x$.} By the end of Step 2, the configuration is $L_{n-1} \cup \{-m e_1\}$. 
We use the induction hypothesis to form $V {\setminus} \{x\}$ from the $L_{n-1}$ subset, where $x$ is a non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$ such that $V {\setminus} \{x\} \in \mathrm{NonIso}_{d,n-1}$.

The use of the induction hypothesis guarantees that there is a sequence of $4^d(n-1)^2 r$ HAT steps from $L_{n-1}$, which: (i) result in $(V{\setminus}\{x\}) \cup \{-m e_1\}$; (ii) have positive activation components; and (iii) have transport steps that are realized by random walk paths with lengths of at most $4^d (n-1) r$, which remain inside $B(r+d(n-1))$.


 \item[Step 4:] {\em Transport the element at $-m e_1$ to $x$.} We activate the element at $-m e_1$ and transport it to $x$, which is possible because $x$ is non-isolated and exposed in $V$. Because $V{\setminus}\{x\}$ lies in $B(r)$, Lemma \ref{kesten cor} implies that there is a path from $-m e_1$ to $x$ which avoids $V{\setminus}\{x\}$, has a length of at most $\ell = 4^d n r$, and lies in $B(r+dn-1)$.
 \end{itemize}

Note that Steps 1 and 2 require $r+dn$ HAT steps, the activation components of which are positive and the transport components of which can be realized by paths of length at most $r+dn \leq \ell$. Steps 3 and 4 require $4^d(n-1)^2 r + 1$ HAT steps, again with positive activation components and transport components realized by paths of length at most $\ell$. In total, at most $M = 4^d n^2 r$ HAT steps are needed and, since all paths lie in $B(r+dn-1)$, conclusions (i) through (iii) hold.

nodes.name: Case 2 construction
nodes.statement:
{\em Case 2}. Because we cannot remove a non-isolated element of $V$ without obtaining an isolated set---a set to which the induction hypothesis does not apply---we must instead use the induction hypothesis to form a set related to $V$. In fact, the first two steps are the same as in Case 1, so we begin with the configuration $L_{n-1} \cup \{-m e_1\}$ and specify the third and subsequent steps.

\begin{itemize}
\item[Step 3':] {\em Use the induction hypothesis.} Let $w$ and $y$ be the least and greatest elements of $V$ in the lexicographic order, and let $x$ be any non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$. We use the induction hypothesis to form
\[
V' = (V {\setminus} \{x,y\}) \cup \{w-e_1\},
\]
which is possible because $V' \in \mathrm{\widehat{N}onIso}_{d,n-1}$.

 The result is a sequence of $4^d(n-1)^2 r$ HAT steps from $L_{n-1}$ which form $V' \cup \{-m e_1\}$ with positive activation components and transport components which are realized by random walk paths with the same properties as in Step 3.

\item[Step 4':] {\em Activate the element at $-m e_1$ and transport it to $w-2e_1$.} 

\item[Step 5':] {\em Treadmill the pair $\{w-e_1,w-2e_1\}$.} Since $w$ is the least element of $V$ in the lexicographic order, $w-e_1$ and $w-2e_1$ are the only elements which lie in $O_1 = \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: z \cdot e_1 \leq w \cdot e_1\}$. Similarly, due to the choice of $y$, it is the only element which lies in $O_2 = \{ z \in \mathbb{Z}^d: z \cdot e_d \geq y \cdot e_d\}$. 

Consequently, it is possible to treadmill the pair $\{w-e_1,w-2e_1\}$ to:
\begin{itemize}
\item $B(r+3)^{\mathsf{c}}$ without leaving $O_1$; then
\item $O_2$ without leaving $B(r+6) {\setminus} B(r + 3)$; and
\item $\{y,y+e_d\}$ without leaving $O_2$.
\end{itemize}
This requires at most $f_2 = 10 r$ HAT steps, each of which has a positive activation component and a transport component realized by a random walk path of length five.

\item[Step 6':] {\em Activate at $\{y+e_d\}$ and transport to $x$.} The configuration at the end of Step 5' is $(V {\setminus} \{x\}) \cup \{y+e_d\}$, so activating the element at $\{y+e_d\}$ and transporting it to $x$ (which is possible because $x$ is an exposed, non-isolated element of $\partial_{\mathrm{exp}} V$), forms $V$.  
\end{itemize}

Recall that Steps 1 and 2 require $r+dn$ HAT steps, which can be realized by paths of length at most $r+dn \leq \ell$. Steps 3' and 4' require $4^d(n-1)^2r + 1$ HAT steps, realized by paths of length at most $\ell$. Steps 5' and 6' require $10r+1$ HAT steps, with paths satisfying the same length bound. All activation components are positive. At most $M$ HAT steps are needed in total and, since all paths lie in $B(r+dn-1)$, conclusions (i) through (iii) hold.
